docs.title: CampusPool
docs.text: CampusPool helps members of the Thapar community coordinate shared rides and find company for campus activities. This is a UCS503 Software Engineering project at TIET.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Sign in with a one-time code sent to a Thapar email address.
  2. Post a ride or activity, or request to join an existing one.
  3. Once connected, use chat to coordinate. For completed rides, the app records each rider's share of the actual fare and lets the ride creator confirm payment.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The Next.js frontend calls a FastAPI backend backed by PostgreSQL. WebSockets deliver live updates, and the browser encrypts one-to-one chat messages before sending them.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A suitable topic needs a defined user group and a workflow that can be demonstrated.

docs.title: Solution

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team planned the frontend, backend and activity work following the design review.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Planned the frontend structure and ride-module implementation tasks.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Frontend and backend work depend on a shared understanding of request fields and responses.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Agree on the inputs, validation messages and returned states for each core workflow.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team implemented the first working components of the application.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Worked on ride creation and discovery screens and frontend navigation.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Account access and data validation affect every protected workflow.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Use the existing API contract, validate required fields and make authentication state visible in the interface.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Connect participation requests and ride settlement to the interface.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The next increment connected user decisions to participation and fare records.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Integrated ride requests, approval actions and request-status screens with the APIs.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: An accepted request consumes capacity. Opening a UPI link and confirming receipt are separate events.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Show request states in the interface. Track rider acknowledgement separately from organiser payment confirmation.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Review integration edge cases and keep the project files organised.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The schedule included a buffer week around a holiday period.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Reviewed pending frontend integration issues and organised repository files.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Integration review needs to account for missing data, stale state and rejected actions.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Record each issue with its triggering action, affected component and expected response before applying fixes.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Check the complete workflows and prepare the second prototype.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team prepared the application for the next prototype and organised the course repository.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Checked the ride workflow, worked on integration fixes and coordinated upload of the application into the GitHub course template.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The course repository combines application code, documentation, journals and reports in distinct folders.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Place the application under code/ and retain the course documentation structure. Exclude local credentials, development encryption keys and uploaded user files from Git.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Prepare the second prototype demonstration and deployment.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The second prototype milestone combined the application workflows and hosting setup.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Integrated the second prototype, worked on deployment and demonstrated the main workflow.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A hosted build depends on consistent frontend routing, backend configuration, database access and email delivery.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Use the Docker and Render configuration, supply deployment settings through environment variables and review the sign-in and ride workflow on the hosted build.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: After the Diwali break, address the final issues and prepare the evaluation material.

docs.text: After the Diwali break, address the final issues and prepare the evaluation material.

docs.title: Week 16 - Final preparation after Diwali break
Problem
docs.text: The team allocated one working week after the Diwali break for final improvements.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Worked on report formatting, screenshots and final activity checks.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The evaluation needs a repeatable demonstration supported by the submitted repository and documentation.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Prepare a consistent account, ride and activity walkthrough. Review configuration, report wording and submission links against the build being demonstrated.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Present the final prototype during evaluation.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The final milestone covered the prototype presentation and explanation of individual contributions.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Prepared explanations of the activity workflow, diagrams and report documentation.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The presentation should connect the problem, design decisions and implementation using one understandable example.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Walk through the main user flow and explain the responsibility of each component.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Keep the final project files and documentation organised for reference.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team compared the shortlisted ideas and selected CampusPool.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Participated in topic selection and discussed non-travel activity coordination.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Rides and activities share discovery and approval steps. Fare settlement belongs to the ride workflow.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Define the common create, discover, request and approve flow. Add fare calculation after ride completion.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Refine the project pitch and investigate existing coordination methods.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team refined the idea and presented CampusPool to the course instructor.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Prepared the feature list and recorded points discussed after the pitch.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The pitch needs to explain who uses the system, what they do and how the project can be demonstrated.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Use a concrete ride example from publication to an organiser decision, then explain the activity variation.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Translate the agreed scope into a proposal and requirements.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The proposal recorded the problem, objectives, scope and proposed engineering approach.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Worked on the scope section, proposal formatting and compilation.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Requirements need observable behaviour so that later diagrams and tests can refer to them.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Describe actor actions and system responses, then check that each core workflow is covered in the proposal.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Prepare the behavioural diagrams for the agreed requirements.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team modelled actors, actions and responsibilities before implementation.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Prepared the swimlane diagram to show which actor performs each step.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A request and its approval are separate actions performed by different actors.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Keep approval decisions with the organiser and show the resulting system update after the decision.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Use the behavioural flows to develop the structural model and data flow diagrams.

docs.title: Week 6 - Class and data flow models
Problem
docs.text: The team developed the class diagram and DFD levels and reviewed their consistency.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Prepared the DFD Level 0 context diagram and checked external entities and diagram labels.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The class model describes relationships, while DFD levels describe how information moves through processes.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Check that account, ride, request, activity and settlement concepts have consistent names across models.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Document message ordering with sequence diagrams and prepare the prototype report.

docs.title: Week 7 - First prototype and sequence diagrams
Problem
docs.text: The first prototype milestone brought together the design models and workflow walkthrough.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Prepared the non-travel activity sequence diagram and compiled the prototype report.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Sequence diagrams must include unsuccessful paths and show when state changes become visible.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Review validation, approval and rejection paths. Keep activity participation outside the fare workflow.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Use prototype feedback to prepare an improvement plan.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The team reviewed the first prototype and planned the next implementation increment.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Maintained feedback notes and identified documentation corrections.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A broad feature request needs to be reduced to a specific change that can be checked.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Group feedback by workflow, identify the affected component and write an acceptance condition for each task.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Review the design during the MST period and prioritise implementation tasks.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The course schedule allocated this period to MST work and design review.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Reviewed activity requirements and the relevant diagrams.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Design review can expose inconsistent field names or transitions before integration begins.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Compare the requirements with the diagrams and record points that need clarification before implementation.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Prepare a small set of implementation tasks for the next increment.
